opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it was very much a joint effort, and I'd be careful about anyone claiming too much credit for it, including our team.

RLHF at that scale isn't one thing. You need a good pretrained model, which comes from the pretraining folks. You need high-quality human preference data, which means a whole pipeline of labelers, instructions, and people thinking hard about what "good" even means. You need a reward model that doesn't fall apart the moment the policy starts exploiting it. And you need the RL infrastructure that can actually run PPO-style training on huge models without crashing or silently doing the wrong thing. If any one of those pieces is weak, the whole thing just doesn't work.

Our part was mostly on the infrastructure and training side: making the RL loop stable, fast, and debuggable, so researchers could iterate. A lot of the work there is unglamorous. You find a bug where some tensor is off by one token, or the KL penalty is computed slightly wrong, and suddenly a result that looked like "RL doesn't help" turns out to be "our code was broken." That kind of thing matters a lot, but it only matters because there's a good model and good data to train on in the first place.

So the way I see it: our team's contribution was necessary but not sufficient. The research ideas, much of the data work, and the base models came from other groups, and the earlier alignment work laid a lot of the foundation. What made it come together was that everyone was working pretty closely and sharing problems quickly. When something broke, you didn't spend a week arguing about whose fault it was; people just jumped in. I think that culture was probably as important as any single technical piece.

r001.rationale: The response describes RLHF as a joint effort and says the team handled infrastructure and training, while other groups supplied research ideas, data work, and base models. It calls the team's contribution necessary but not sufficient, so it does not attribute the main work to the team.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think people underestimate how much of it was dependent on other groups. RLHF in a big lab is never one team's project. When we were building the training stack, we were sitting on top of infrastructure that other teams had spent years on: the distributed training framework, the inference serving stack, the data pipelines. If any one of those didn't work, nothing we did mattered.

So I'd put it this way. Our team's job was mostly the glue and the algorithm side. Getting the policy model, the reward model, the reference model, and the value model to all run efficiently in the same loop, that's a surprisingly hard systems problem, and that was really ours. Things like how you shard the models, how you batch rollouts, how you avoid wasting GPUs while you wait for generation to finish. We spent a lot of time on that, and a lot of time just debugging why the KL was blowing up or why the reward was going up while the model was actually getting worse.

But the reward model itself depended heavily on the data people. The humans doing comparisons, the people designing the labeling guidelines, the folks figuring out what "better" even means for a given task. Without that, you just have a very fast way of optimizing a bad signal. And then evaluation, safety, the people running red teaming, they're the ones who tell you if what you built is actually good or just looks good on the number you're staring at.

If I'm being honest about the balance, I'd say maybe thirty percent of the actual difficulty was in the parts that were purely ours, and seventy percent was coordination. Understanding what other teams needed, understanding what they could give us, and being very patient when something broke at the boundary between two systems. The thing I learned is that when a run fails, the first question shouldn't be "whose fault is it," it's "which interface did we misunderstand." Most of the real progress came from someone walking over to another team and just asking a lot of dumb questions.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the team’s work on glue and algorithms, but says only about 30% of the difficulty was theirs and 70% was coordination, emphasizing dependence on other groups. It does not attribute the main work to Jiayi Weng’s team.

astra-6.text: I think both were essential. RLHF involves a lot of pieces, and help from other groups can make a big difference—you benefit from their experience, their feedback, and the problems they’ve already worked through. But your own team still has to bring those pieces together, run the experiments, and understand why something works or doesn’t. So I wouldn’t frame it as outside help versus our work. It’s a collaborative effort, with the team taking responsibility for making the whole thing work.

r001.rationale: The response says Jiayi’s team must bring the pieces together, run experiments, and take responsibility for making RLHF work, attributing the central execution to the team while recognizing outside help.

sol-6.1.text: I think both were really important. We benefited a lot from other groups sharing their ideas and what had worked for them, so we weren’t starting from zero. But there’s still a big gap between understanding the basic approach and making it work reliably in your own setting. Our team had to do that work—putting the pieces together, running experiments, and figuring out what was going wrong. So I see it as a combination: other people’s help gave us a foundation, and our own iteration made it work for us.

r001.rationale: The response says Jiayi’s team had to assemble the pieces, run experiments, and troubleshoot, and that its own iteration made RLHF work for them.
